column1: And India's job is harder than China's.
China's A.I. mostly needs one written language.
Our country's Constitution lists twenty-two, written in about a dozen different scripts.
Each one needs its own shelf.
And that's why your question cost so much more in Hindi, Marathi and Telugu.
Remember the chopper?
It learns its pieces from this same library.
Words it sees all the time, like rain or village, become one neat piece each.
Your words, which it hardly ever sees, get chopped into bits.
Sometimes into half a letter.
Here's the rule.
A machine learns from what it reads.
And what goes wrong?
If our language is only a tiny corner of the library, the machine learns it last... and charges us more.
So someone has to build the Indian part of the library.
Page by page, voice by voice.
And that's slow, expensive work.
And India has started.
A government data shelf for Indian builders, called A.I.
Kosh, now holds more than sixteen thousand collections.
But words are only half of it.
Even with a perfect library, you need a place to read it.
And this is where India hits a wall.
This is the reading room.
A chip like this one, made by an American company called Nvidia.
It's called a G.P.U., and a single one costs lakhs of rupees.
And to train a big A.I., you need thousands of them, wired together, running for months.
And here's the catch.
India doesn't make these chips.
They're designed in America and made mostly in Taiwan.
If you watched our chip film, you know why.
